passages.text: Differentiation of Aspartic and Isoaspartic Acid Using 193 nm Ultraviolet Photodissociation Mass Spectrometry

Spontaneous conversion of aspartic acid (Asp) to isoaspartic acid (isoAsp) is a ubiquitous modification that influences the structure and function of proteins. This modification of Asp impacts the stability of biotherapeutics and has been linked to the development of neurodegenerative diseases. We explored the use of 193 nm ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD) to distinguish Asp and isoAsp in the protonated and deprotonated peptides. The differences in the relative abundances of several fragment ions uniquely generated by UVPD were used to differentiate isomeric peptide standards containing Asp or isoAsp. These fragment ions result from the cleavage of bonds N-terminal to Asp/isoAsp residues in addition to the side-chain losses from Asp/isoAsp or the losses of, , , or  from -ions. Fragmentation of Asp-containing tryptic peptides using UVPD resulted in more enhanced  ions, while isoAsp-containing peptides yielded more enhanced  ions. UVPD was also used to identify an isomerized peptide from a tryptic digest of a monoclonal antibody. Moreover, UVPD of a protonated nontryptic peptide resulted in more enhanced  ions N- and C-terminal to isoAsp and differences in  ion ratios that were used to identify the isoAsp peptide.
Graphical Abstract
INTRODUCTION

Isomerization of aspartic acid (Asp, D) and deamidation of asparagine (Asn, N) to isoaspartic acid (isoAsp) via the formation of a succinimide intermediate are two aberrant in vivo modifications that play key roles in the pathways of neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and other amyloid diseases. Racemization of the succinimide intermediate is also possible, leading to the formation of two additional isomers (D-Asp and D-isoAsp). Although racemization is more prevalent in long-lived proteins such as those found in the eye lens, formation of D-Asp and D-isoAsp in synthetic peptides has been detected upon asparagine deamidation. Isomerization of Asp and deamidation of Asn occur spontaneously, adding an extra methylene group to the peptide backbone which may lead to aggregation, alter the structure, or result in the loss of protein function. These modifications also occur in vitro after the isolation of therapeutic proteins and pose challenges in the manufacturing of stable biotherapeutics. Physical and chemical stress during manufacturing and storage leads to the degradation of protein therapeutics or loss of activity. The isomerization of Asp and deamidation of Asn in the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are the major degradation pathways that lead to the loss of target binding and ultimately their potency.- It is well known that exposure to high temperatures and high pH accelerates deamidation, oxidation, enzymatic cleavages, dimer formation, and aggregation of proteins. Therefore, protein therapeutics are generally stored under mildly acidic pH (4-6) conditions which in turn favor isomerization. Studies aimed at deciphering the factors that modulate Asp/Asn isomerization have shown that peptides and proteins containing nonbulky amino acids, primarily Gly, at the carboxyl side of Asn/Asp are more susceptible to isomerization and deamidation reactions. - CDRs and other regions of mAbs that are particularly flexible and/or have higher solvent accessibilities are also more prone to deamidation and isomerization.

Considering the impact of Asn/Asp isomerization, identification of the resulting isomerized residues is vital for unraveling disease mechanisms and for the comprehensive characterization of biotherapeutics prior to an investigational new drug application filing at the Food and Drug Administration or other foreign regulatory agency. While deamidation results in a mass shift of 0.984 Da and can be easily detected using mass spectrometry (MS), isomerization is difficult to detect because there is no mass change associated with it. Several tandem MS (MS/MS)-based methods have been developed to address the challenging differentiation of Asp/isoAsp in proteins.- In one of the earlier reports, low-energy CID was used to identify isoAsp peptides based on the presence of diagnostic  (is the position of isoAsp) and  ions ( is the length of the peptide), depending on the location of the basic residue. Collision-based methods produce more abundant fragment ions from the cleavage adjacent to isoAsp residues than from the cleavage adjacent to Asp residues. Asp/isoAsp peptides can therefore be differentiated by comparing the differences in the intensities of  ions formed directly adjacent to the Asp/ isoAsp residues. These differences, however, are not observed for all isoAsp-containing peptides. Among the most successful, electron capture dissociation (ECD) and electron transfer transfer dissociation (ETD) can differentiate isoAsp from Asp based on the production of two diagnostic fragment ions (and) which are not generated from Asp peptides.- These electron-based activation methods are ideally suited for multiple charged peptides; however, charge reduction is dominant for low charge states. To aid the quantitation of low-abundance isoAsp modifications, Asp-N protease was used to selectively cleave N-terminal Asp residues generating smaller peptides, while isoAsp-containing sections of the protein remained as larger peptides, and ETD was used to distinguish them from Asp peptides without interference from Asp peptides. Another study reported the evaluation of several fragmentation methods to differentiate Asp/isoAsp peptides. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization postsource decay (MALDI-PSD) generated a low-abundance but diagnostic  ion only from the isoAsp peptide and enhanced  ions N-terminal to isoAsp. In addition to the enhanced  ions N-terminal to isoAsp, 157 nm photodissociation (PD) also generated low-abundance but unique  and  ions from Asp peptides but not from the corresponding isoAsp peptides. These unusual -type ions are formed by side-chain losses from  radical ions (Scheme S1a,b). Introducing a fixed charge in the N-terminus, the peptides also generated enhanced  ions N-terminal to isoAsp upon MALDIPSD/157 nm PD. Reactions with carbodiimides, well-characterized carboxylic acid coupling reagents, yielded peptides that produced different ratios of specific fragment ions that allowed differentiation of Asp and isoAsp using CID. Radical-directed dissociation (RDD) has also been successfully applied for the identification of isoAsp. In this method, iodobenzoyl-labeled peptides were irradiated with a UV photon to generate a highly reactive peptide radical which was selectively fragmented using CID. Additionally, MALDI-LIFT-TOF/TOF was used for the determination and relative quantitation of singly and doubly isomerized (Asp7 and Asp23) versions of synthetic amyloid  peptides and identification of isoAsp residues in thermally degraded mAb based on the ratios of  ions formed by the cleavage of the bond N-terminal to Asp/isoAsp.

In addition to the extensive evaluation of MS/MS methods to differentiate Asp and isoAsp peptides, efforts have also focused on separating the peptide isomers using ion mobility spectrometry MS (IMS-MS). Structures for lossless ion manipulations (SLIM)-MS were used to separate four isomers of synthetic -peptide containing D and L forms of Asp and isoAsp. More recently, high-resolution demultiplexing was used to improve the resolution of drift tube IMS-MS separation, enabling the identification of seven of the eight isomeric Asp and isoAsp peptide pairs investigated. CID in conjunction with cyclic IMS-MS was used to differentiate and identify the site of isoAsp formation in three synthetic peptides. More recently, a workflow was established to differentiate isomers based on the differences in the relative intensities between common fragment ions found in the MS/ MS spectra generated using CID, HCD, ETD, and RDD. For this workflow, replicate spectra were collected for several different peptides and their isomers while intentionally varying the instrumental parameters to establish a statistical threshold that allows the confident assignment of isomers. This extensive and systematic study affirmed that isomeric peptides could be successfully differentiated based on small differences in intensities of fragment ions common between the isomers.

The application of 193 nm ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD) for the characterization of a variety of post-translational modifications of proteins has been reported.- 193 nm UVPD has been particularly useful for localizing sites of PTMs because of the rich array of fragment ions (, , , , , and ), extensive backbone cleavages which afford highsequence coverage, and retention of labile modifications. Moreover, the performance of UVPD is less dependent on the charge state of the precursor compared to the more significant charge state dependence of collision- and electron-based activation methods, making UVPD well suited for the analysis of singly or doubly charged peptides in positive or negative polarity.- Most of the MS/MS-based studies reported thus far utilize positive polarity.- Since negative mode UVPD has been reported to provide complementary results to increase the depth of proteome coverage in bottom-up MS, it is worthwhile to characterize the Asp/isoAsp-containing peptides (which contain at least one negatively charged residue) in negative mode. Herein, we investigate the potential of 193 nm UVPD to differentiate isomeric peptides containing Asp/isoAsp in both positive and negative polarities.
EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
Direct Infusion and Tandem Mass Spectrometry (MS/MS).

For direct infusion experiments, peptide samples were prepared at a concentration of 10 muM in 50:50 methanol:water, with 0.5% formic acid (v/v), and infused using static emitters. All spectra were acquired on a Thermo Fisher Scientific Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (San Jose, CA) modified with an excimer laser to enable 193 nm UVPD as previously described. The spectra were acquired in both positive and negative polarities using a spray voltage of 0.9 to 1 kV. Both MS and MS/MS experiments were performed at a resolution of 120,000 at  200. One hundred spectra were averaged for each spectrum (25 scans with 4 micro-scans per scan). MS/MS experiments were acquired using an isolation width of 2  and an AGC target of 5 x 105 charges. 193 nm UVPD was performed using 2 pulses of 3 mJ each or as indicated. The pulse energy is measured at the laser, and only a fraction of the unfocused beam irradiates the ions owing to the beam restriction and high divergence of the laser. Details about the heat stressing procedure and digestion of monoclonal antibody (mAb), as well as the LC-MS/MS parameters and data analysis, are included in the Supporting Information.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Identification of IsoAsp in Peptide Standards Using 193 nm UVPD.

Seven pairs of isomeric peptides (ALDGK, ADLGK, ALDEK, GLDLLK, GDLLLK, GFSYTDANK, and VVSLTVLHQDWLNGK, where the D in bold font represents the position of the Asp/isoAsp residue) were characterized by ESI-UVPD-MS in both positive and negative modes. The monoisotopic masses and observed charge states are summarized in Table S1. In positive polarity, peptides ALDGK, ADLGK, ALDEK, GLDLLK, GDLLLK, and GFSYTDANK were observed in  and 1+ charge states, while the peptide VVSLTVLHQDWLNGK was observed in  and 3+ charge states (Figure S1). In negative polarity, peptides ALDGK, ADLGK, ALDEK, GLDLLK, GDLLLK, and GFSYTDANK were primarily singly charged (1-), whereas VVSLTVLHQDWLNGK was primarily doubly charged (2-) (Figure S2).

Fragmentation of ALDGK and ALisoDGK peptides in positive and negative modes (Figure 1) using 193 nm UVPD generated similar ion types, but the peptides varied in relative abundances. The spectra predominantly contained -type ions and exhibited fewer  ions. Neutral losses of  (43.9898 Da), (44.9977 Da), and  (18.0106 Da) from the precursor were observed from both the protonated (Figures 1a,b and S3-S7) and deprotonated peptides (Figures 1c,d and S8-S13). These neutral loss ions were generally more enhanced for the isoAsp peptides, particularly for the deprotonated peptides. IsoAsp peptides also resulted in more abundant neutral losses of, , , and  from  or  ions compared to Asp peptides for both polarities, and these neutral losses from the  ions were more prominent for the deprotonated peptides.

As also observed upon collisional activation, UVPD generated more enhanced  ions from cleavages adjacent to isoAsp for protonated peptides (Figures 1, S3-S7). For example, the abundances of  and  ions were increased for protonated ALisoDGK. Consistent with the mobile proton model which rationalizes the prominence of backbone cleavages C-terminal to Asp when peptides have few protons or the protons are sequestered at basic residues, fragmentation C-terminal to Asp is the most abundant feature for the protonated peptides (ALDGK, ADLGK, ALDEK, GLDLLK, and GDLLLK). As noted previously, and  ions were more favorably generated by cleavage N-terminal to isoAsp than from Asp for protonated peptides.

In contrast to 157 nm UVPD that generated low-abundance  ion only from Asp-containing peptides, 193 nm UVPD generated  ion also from three of the five isoAsp peptides analyzed in positive mode (Figures 1 and S3-S7). Additionally, ions (i.e., fragment ions shifted by 1.0078 Da from the standard  ions) were observed for the protonated Asp peptides but were absent in the corresponding isoAsp peptides. Both  and  ions were generated from all six deprotonated peptides (Asp and isoAsp) but with higher abundances for the Asp peptides (Figures 1 and S8-S13). However, other side-chain loss ions, such as  ions, were not generated by the fragmentation of the protonated or deprotonated Asp/isoAsp peptides using 193 nm UVPD. According to the proposed mechanisms, and  side-chain loss ions are formed from the  radical ions during 157 nm UVPD. Loss of CONH and a radical fragment from the Asp side chain results in the formation of  ions (Scheme S1a), while the complete loss of the Asp side chain (as a  radical) and a  group results in the formation of  ions (Scheme S1b). Since the  group of the isoAsp residue is a part of the peptide backbone, the resultant  ion is 14 Da heavier than the one generated from an Asp peptide (Scheme S1c). The mass of this  ion from the isoAsp peptide is exactly equal to the mass of the  ion generated by the loss of the side chain , followed by the loss of hydrogen from the  ion of the corresponding Asp peptide (Scheme S2). As a result, this ion (or) may originate from different pathways and result in products of identical  values and thus may not differentiate the Asp/ isoAsp peptides (Figure 1, inset). 157 nm UVPD resulted in the formation of more abundant  ions from protonated isoAsp peptides than from Asp peptides. For 193 nm UVPD, the  and  ions were more enhanced for both protonated and deprotonated isoAsp peptides (Figure 1b,d inset, and Figures S3a-S13a).

The UVPD mass spectra of both protonated and deprotonated peptide isomers (Figures S3-S13) are similar but with some differences in the relative abundances of specific fragment ions. These differences are primarily noted in the C-terminal fragment ions  that result from backbone cleavages N-terminal to Asp/isoAsp residues in addition to those ions resulting from the loss of, , , or. To highlight the variations in the fragmentation patterns of the Asp and isoAsp peptides, the differences in TIC (total ion current) abundances for these key fragment ions were calculated (Difference = (TIC abundance of Asp - TIC abundance of isoAsp)/TIC abundance of Asp), and the values are plotted as histograms in Figure 2.

For the protonated peptides (Figure 2a), the, , , , , , and  ions are enhanced for nearly all of the isoAsp peptides (with a few outliers highlighted) and can be used to differentiate isoAsp peptides from Asp peptides. Although 193 nm UVPD did not generate  ions exclusively from all Asp peptides, the  ions were enhanced for Asp peptides and were absent for the ALisoDGK and GisoDLLLK peptides. Likewise, the  ions were not observed for protonated ALisoDEK, GLisoDLLK, and GisoDLLLK and were enhanced for all of the Asp peptides. Therefore, the higher abundances of  and  ions can be used as diagnostic markers for Asp peptides.

For deprotonated peptides (Figure 2b), the TIC abundances of, , , , , , and  ions were greater for isoAsp peptides, with a few outliers highlighted. While the abundances of  and  ions were elevated for Asp peptides, they are generated from both Asp and isoAsp peptides for all six peptides. In contrast to the UVPD patterns of the protonated peptides, the  and  ions were almost exclusively generated from deprotonated Asp peptides and not from isoAsp peptides (black triangles). Overall, the differences in the UVPD spectra were more notable for deprotonated peptides compared to those for protonated peptides. In order to evaluate the ability to quantify the Asp/isoAsp ratios using negative mode UVPD, calibration curves were created for four peptide pairs (Asp and isoAsp isomers of ALDGK, ADLGK, GLDLLK, and GDLLLK) based on the abundance of key fragment ions (specifically, , , , , and  ions) as a function of the composition of the mixtures (Figures S14-S17). The results fit a linear trend line with  with a few exceptions (of 0.976 for the  ion of ALDGK, of 0.804 for the  ion of ADLGK, of 0.777 for the  ion of GLDLLK, and  of 0.765 for the  ion of GDLLLK). Other product ions did not follow a linear trend. Additionally, the slopes varied based on the peptide sequence. Therefore, this method was not sufficiently robust for quantitative analysis. Because  and  ions have proven to be diagnostic for isoAsp peptides in prior ETD/ ECD studies,- we also searched for these ions in the UVPD spectra, but they were only rarely or inconsistently found.

A ratiometric strategy developed to identify epimers and isomers has been used for the differentiation of Asp and isoAsp peptides. In this method, a pair of fragment ions with differences in abundance between the isomeric spectra is selected to calculate the R-isomer value, according to eq 1

In eq 1, and  are the intensities of fragment ions 1 and 2 from the spectrum of a peptide, and  and  are the intensities of fragment ions 1 and 2 from the spectrum of its isomer. The calculation of R-isomer values was automated by the development of a software tool to consider many combinations of fragment ions, thus allowing enhanced differences in the production of diagnostic pairs of fragment ions to be more readily pinpointed. Theoretically, R-isomer values for two identical peptides should be 1.0, but to account for the variability in signal intensities, a threshold of 1.9 was applied for CID spectra and 2.4 for radical-directed dissociation (RDD) spectra. A larger R-isomer value corresponds to a greater difference in the fragmentation between Asp and isoAsp peptides. This tool was adopted in the present study to assess a list of diagnostic ions (, , , , , , and) to calculate R-isomer values for all possible ion pair combinations. A threshold value of 2.4 was sufficient to distinguish the Asp and isoAsp peptide isomers for UVPD, as the R-isomer value calculated for the replicate spectra of a peptide was lower than 1.2 for all of the ion pairs examined. R-isomer values were calculated for ion pairs that were present across five sets of isomeric peptides, as listed in Table S2. In Table S2, the R-isomer values are significantly higher for the deprotonated peptides than for the protonated peptides. More notably, the R-isomer values of 10 specific ion pairs generated from the deprotonated peptides are much higher and are shown in a bar graph (Figure 3). R-isomer values for a set of seven ion pairs detected for at least three protonated peptides are summarized in a bar graph (Figure S18). These values show less significant variations than those calculated for the corresponding deprotonated peptides, confirming that differentiation of Asp- and isoAsp peptides should be more successful by the examination of deprotonated peptides.

To further evaluate the performance of UVPD to distinguish the isomeric peptides, we compared the R-isomer values for  ion pairs generated by UVPD of protonated peptides relative to the values reported by MALDI-LIFT-TOF/TOF in a prior study, as summarized in Table S3. The R-isomer values calculated using either of the fragmentation methods were comparable. We also evaluated the R-isomer values for additional  ion pairs uniquely resulting from cleavages adjacent to the Asp/isoAsp residues. The R-isomer value for the  ion pair for peptide ALDGK is 17.8 and that for the  ion pair for GLDLLK is 24.8. Similarly, the R-isomer value for the  ion pair for peptide ALDEK is 5.5. These values are much larger than the threshold value of 2.4, enabling more confident isomer identification. However, the  ion pair for ADLGK resulted in an R-isomer value of only 1.1, which is significantly lower than the threshold value. For this pair, the very low abundance of the  ion might have skewed the outcome. Overall, the magnitude of the R-values was larger for deprotonated peptides than for protonated peptides, again suggesting that UVPD of deprotonated peptides is the preferred strategy for the characterization of Asp/isoAsp peptides.
Identification of IsoAsp in a Mixture of Peptides using 193 nm UVPD.

We next sought to differentiate Aspand isoAsp-containing peptides in a mixture of six pairs of isomeric peptides: ALDGK, ADLGK, ALDEK, GLDLLK, GDLLLK, and VVSLTVLHQDWLNGK. The peptides were separated using reversed-phase chromatography and subjected to targeted UVPD (3 mJ/2 pulses) in both positive and negative polarity. The base peak chromatogram for the peptide mixture is shown in Figure S19, and the extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) of the peptides ionized in negative mode are shown in Figure S20. The isoAsp versions of peptides ALDGK and ADLGK (,  501.27, green trace) are baseline-separated from the unmodified forms. However, the peptides ALDEK/ALisoDEK (,  573.29, blue trace) elute almost at the same time as ALDGK/ALisoDGK/ ADLGK/AisoDLGK (2.6 min) These three peptides and their isoAsp forms all eluted within 2-3 min of each other with baseline separation between each isomeric pair. The chromatographic peaks corresponding to the pairs of peptides, GLDLLK and GDLLK (,  656.40), are also baseline-resolved and eluted much later between 14 and 18 min. The peptide pair VVSLTVLHQDWLNGK (,  852.96) eluted between 41 and 42 min. Since the elution order of the Asp/ isoAsp peptides is not always consistent, UVPD was used to assign the identities based on the inspection of the fragmentation patterns acquired in the positive and negative modes. Based on the strategy detailed in the prior sections, UVPD spectra were searched for differences in abundances of key fragment ions that allowed the identification of peptide sequence and differentiation of Asp/isoAsp residues (Figures S21-29). For example, LC peaks 3 and 4 were assigned as ALisoDEK and ALDEK, respectively, based on the presence of enhanced  ion for the first peptide (deprotonated) and enhanced  ions for the second peptide (also deprotonated) (Figure S23). The elution order and identities of the peptides in the mixture and a summary of the fragment ions used to identify and differentiate the Asp/ isoAsp peptides are shown in Table S4. The peptide assignments were verified by comparing the UVPD spectra collected for the standard peptides.
Application of 193 nm UVPD to Distinguish isoAsp Peptide from a Tryptic Digest of a Monoclonal Antibody.

To demonstrate the broader scope of the UVPD strategy, it was applied to monitor the aspartate isomerization of the antipertussis toxin antibody (hu1B7). Heat stress (pH 7.8 at 40  C for 4 weeks) was used to accelerate the degradation and potential isomerization of this antibody prior to tryptic digestion and analysis. The base peak chromatograms of the control and heat-stressed samples are shown in Figure S30. The sequences of the heavy chain (HC) and the light chain (LC) of hu1B7 and the peptide coverage map are shown in Figure S31. The samples were first subjected to HCD (NCE = 28%), and the EICs of Asp-containing peptides were examined for the control and heat-stressed samples. Among 11 Asp-containing tryptic peptides from the HC, three (present in both control and stressed samples) were selected for targeted analysis using UVPD (Table S5): SEDTAVYYC[+57.021]TR (682.79,), FNWYVDGVEVHNAK (839.41,), and GFYPSDIAVEWESNGQPENNYK (1273.08,). EICs were generated to monitor each of the three  values of the peptides in both the control and heat-stressed samples (Figure 4 and Figure S32). Isomerization products were either not observed or were not chromatographically resolved for SEDTAVYYC[+57.021]TR, as evidenced by a clean EIC (Figure S32a,b; elution time, 25.3 min). A single LC peak is observed in the EIC of the GFYPSDIAVEWESNGQPENNYK peptide for the control sample (Figure S32c), whereas a second peak (much broader) is also observed in the EIC of the heat-stressed sample (Figure S32d; elution time, 51 min). The GFYPSDIAVEWESNGQPENNYK peptide was observed in two charge states, 849.03  and  1273.07 , for the control hu1B7 sample (Figure S33a). The targeted UVPD analysis (1273.07) of the heat-stressed hu1B7 sample resulted in the identification of several spectra corresponding to a deamidated product (1273.5) of high abundance and only a single MS/MS spectrum corresponding to the unmodified precursor of low abundance. Therefore, this peptide was not suitable for Asp/isoAsp analysis using UVPD. The MS1 spectra averaged across the EIC of both peaks in the heat-stressed sample reveal deamidation of Asn/Gln residues (Figure S33b,c). The HCD MS/MS spectra across three regions of the EIC of the same peptide (1273.07) reveal that the first region of the LC peak corresponds to the unmodified peptide, the second slice of the LC peak corresponds to the N14-deamidated peptide, and the third section of the LC peak corresponds to the triply deamidated peptide (N14, Q16, and N19) (Figure S34).

A conserved sequence (FNWYVD281GVEVHNAK) in the fragment-crystallizable region of the heavy chain of hu1B7 proved to be isomerized and was chromatographically resolved, as evidenced in the corresponding EIC (Figure 4a,b; elution time, 40.3 min). Based on manual integration of the two peaks in Figure 4b, the peak area for isoAsp is 5.3 +- 0.8% and that for Asp is 94.7 +- 0.8% (average of three injections). This peptide was primarily observed in the  and  charge states (Figure 4c,d). The MS1 spectra across both the peaks in the heat-stressed sample show the same  values, suggesting that these are the isomeric species, with the isoAsp peptide eluting prior to the Asp peptide. A targeted method was used to perform UVPD (3 pulses at 3 mJ per pulse) of the FNWYVDGVEVHNAK peptide (839.4,). UVPD primarily generated abundant  ions (Figure S35). The abundances of the  and  ions are enhanced for the isoAsp peptide relative to that of the Asp peptide. In addition, the abundances of five diagnostic C-terminal ions (, , , , and), all in the region between  890 and 970, are more enhanced for the isoAsp peptide (Figure S36). Moreover, the unusual  ion that is produced only from isoAsp peptides using electron-based methods is also generated at a very low abundance only for the isoAsp peptide using UVPD. In contrast, the abundances of  and  ions are slightly enhanced for the Asp peptide, a feature that is more distinctive for UVPD of singly charged peptides.

Although this method performed well for singly charged synthetic peptides, most of the tryptic peptides in the digest were much larger and were observed predominantly in  and  charge states. While an alternative and less specific protease like chymotrypsin can be used to generate smaller peptides, the neutral loss or side-chain loss ions that were used to distinguish isoAsp peptides rely on the presence of a C-terminal lysine. Therefore, we examined the fragmentation pattern of a pair of nontryptic isomeric standard peptides ALDGE and ALisoDGE using ESI-UVPD in positive mode (Figure S37). As observed for tryptic peptides, more enhanced  and  ions were observed for the isoAsp peptide compared to the unmodified ALDGE peptide. Neutral loss of COOH from the precursor was also enhanced for the isoAsp peptide. In contrast to prior observations for tryptic peptides, the  ion was significantly suppressed for the isoAsp peptide, a feature that was also noted upon MALDI-LIFT-TOF/TOF analysis of the same peptide. The ratios of  and  ions are significantly different in the spectra of the two isomeric peptides. These features can potentially be used for the identification of nontryptic isoAsp peptides.
CONCLUSIONS

We have demonstrated that ESI-RPLC-UVPD-MS/MS can be used to distinguish Asp and isoAsp-containing tryptic-like peptides using negative or positive ionization mode based on the differences in TIC abundances of fragment ions uniquely generated by UVPD. These differences were more prominent for deprotonated peptides than for protonated peptides (in both cases as singly charged ions; or 1-). Singly charged Asp-containing peptides resulted in more enhanced  ions, while isoAsp-containing peptides resulted in more enhanced  ions when analyzed using positive or negative mode ESI-UVPD. Although the  ions were not consistently generated for doubly protonated Asp peptides, isoAsp peptides can still be distinguished by monitoring the presence of more abundant  ions N-terminal to the isoAsp residues in positive mode or the presence of more abundant  ions (N-terminal to isoAsp) in negative mode. We also applied this method to identify a doubly protonated isoAsp-containing peptide in a forced degraded mAb digest based on the presence of slightly enhanced  and  produced for the Asp peptide and enhanced, , , , , and  ions for the isoAsp peptide. Although this method is limited to singly charged tryptic peptides for monitoring  and  type ions, singly charged nontryptic peptides containing isoAsp could still be reliably distinguished based on the abundance of  ions.

Ion pairing agents may be used for charge reduction, thus aiding the generation of these diagnostic  type ions from larger peptides using UVPD. The confidence of isoAsp identification is also improved by utilizing both positive and negative mode UVPD in cases where the monitored diagnostic ions are lacking or do not follow the established trends. Additionally, using the protease chymotrypsin should generate smaller peptides, therefore favoring the production of singly charged  ions.

This UVPD-based method has the potential of joining the suite of MS and tandem-MS methods currently being used in biopharmaceutical research to characterize Asp to isoAsp isomerization in biotherapeutics. One can envisage that using the appropriate MS instrumentation that can rapidly switch between polarities and fragmentation methods (electron-based fragmentation and the UVPD method described herein) will allow reliable identification of the presence of isomerized aspartate residues.

passages.text: Intermolecular electron transfer in radical SAM enzymes as a new paradigm for reductive activation

Radical S-adenosyl-L-methionine (rSAM) enzymes bind one or more Fe-S clusters and catalyze transformations that produce complex and structurally diverse natural products. One of the clusters, a 4Fe-4S cluster, binds and reductively cleaves SAM to generate the 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical, which initiates the catalytic cycle by H-atom transfer from the substrate. The role(s) of the additional auxiliary Fe-S clusters (ACs) remains largely enigmatic. The rSAM enzyme PapB catalyzes the formation of thioether cross-links between the beta-carbon of an Asp and a Cys thiolate found in the PapA peptide. One of the two ACs in the protein binds to the substrate thiol where, upon formation of a thioether bond, one reducing equivalent is returned to the protein. However, for the next catalytic cycle to occur, the protein must undergo an electronic state isomerization, returning the electron to the SAM-binding cluster. Using a series of iron-sulfur cluster deletion mutants, our data support a model whereby the isomerization is an obligatorily intermolecular electron transfer event that can be mediated by redox active proteins or small molecules, likely via the second AC in PapB. Surprisingly, a mixture of FMN and NADPH is sufficient to support both the reductive and the isomerization steps. These findings lead to a new paradigm involving intermolecular electron transfer steps in the activation of rSAM enzymes that require multiple iron-sulfur clusters for turnover. The implications of these results for the biological activation of rSAM enzymes are discussed.

Radical S-adenosyl-L-methionine (rSAM) enzymes comprise a superfamily of metalloenzymes that catalyze a wide range of radical-mediated transformations. All rSAM enzymes bind a 4Fe-4S cubane cluster (RS cluster) with three Fe atoms coordinating three Cys thiolate that are nearly always located within a conserved CxxxCxxC motif. The fourth Fe coordinates the alpha-amino and alpha-carboxylate moieties of the SAM cofactor. While the cluster can exist in either the +2 or +1 oxidation states, only the reduced cluster catalyzes the reductive cleavage of SAM to form a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical (dAdo ), which initiates the catalytic cycle of most rSAM enzymes via H-atom transfer from the substrate.

Several classes of rSAM enzymes are recognized. Class 1 enzymes use SAM catalytically, returning the SAM-binding [4Fe-4S] cluster to the +1 state. Class 2 enzymes generate a glycyl radical on a protein substrate. Most rSAM enzymes belong to class 3, which use SAM stoichiometrically. While the RS cluster is housed within a partial TIM barrel, most characterized rSAM enzymes contain additional Fe-S clusters, referred to as auxiliary clusters (ACs), that are housed in C-terminal extensions of the TIM barrel domain. The SPASM-(subtilosin maturase, PQQ maturase, anaerobic sulfatase maturation enzyme, and mycofactocin maturase) domain proteins contain two ACs, while Twitch-domain proteins house one AC. The best characterized RS enzymes containing these AC motifs are those that insert sulfur into their substrate, such as lipoic acid synthase and biotin synthase. In these systems, the AC that is proximal to the RS cluster is the source of the sulfur that is inserted into the substrate. With a few exceptions, the role of the analogous ACs in other rSAM enzymes remain elusive. In the case of SPASM domain-containing rSAM enzymes, the role of the distal cluster remains enigmatic.

The catalytic cycle of all rSAM enzymes requires the reduction of the RS cluster from a catalytically inactive +2 state to the catalytically active +1 state. This reduction is usually mimicked in vitro using strong chemical reductants such as sodium dithionite (NaDT) or titanium citrate. Reichard and colleagues were the first to show that flavodoxin (FldA) and flavodoxin reductase (FPR) can also support turnover by relaying electrons from NADPH. This latter discovery was initially made with the Escherichia coli homologs of the two proteins and has been adopted by most laboratories working on rSAM enzymes. Ironically, this approach is often referred to as using the biologically or physiologically relevant reducing system to activate rSAM enzymes. Although other homologs of FldA and FPR have been used successfully with rSAM enzymes, the pair from E. coli has demonstrated activation of rSAM enzymes from nearly every kingdom of life. However, considering the diverse surface topologies of many radical rSAM enzymes, it seems unlikely that the reducing pair found in E. coli is a universal biological reducing system for all rSAM enzymes, with its successful utilization to date representing exceptions. Indeed, a flavoprotein such as FldA is not the only possible candidate for reducing system in vivo. For example, Booker and colleagues have shown that MiaB from Thermatoga maritima can be activated by an iron-sulfur-containing ferredoxin homolog from the same organism, where the activating electron is ultimately derived from NADPH via a ferredoxin-NADP+ oxidoreductase also from T. maritima. An interesting recent example of a reducing system for rSAM enzymes is a modified yellow fluorescent protein analogue, PSP2, with a photoactivatable prosthetic group. When photoreduced, PSP2 supports turnover of BtrN and Dph2; presumably the organic prosthetic group is the electron donor. Therefore, the key requirement for inactivation of rSAM proteins appears to be the presence of a species that can catalyze one-electron reduction. These observations highlight a crucial gap in understanding how rSAM enzymes are activated in vivo.

Robetta-predicted structural model of PapB and the thioether formation mechanism.A, the conserved Cys residues in the sequence alignment (Fig. S2) are predicted to occur in three distinct regions. The Cys residues that ligate the three 4Fe-4S clusters in PapB are shown in red (RS), yellow (AC1), and purple (AC2). B, upon reduction of the RS cluster, the homolytic cleavage of SAM produces a dAdo . C, the dAdo  abstracts an H-atom from the position alpha to the carboxylate in the peptide, generating a substrate radical. Thioether bond formation is coupled to disengagement from AC1.

PapB (WP_019688962.1) is a class 3, SPASM-domain rSAM enzyme that catalyzes the formation of thioether cross-links between Cys and Asp residues in a ribosomally encoded and posttranslationally modified polypeptide (RiPP), PapA. The genes that encode for PapA and PapB, originating from Paenibacillus polymyxa, are located in adjacent open reading frames (orfs). Previous studies of this system have shown six CX3D motifs in the PapA substrate that are cross-linked by PapB catalysis. However, PapB is active with a peptide substrate that has only one of these CX3D sites (minimal substrate PapA, msPapA), thereby simplifying the biochemical studies of the protein. PapB is among the most active rSAM enzymes and has a robust turnover number of 7.4 s-1. While the structure of PapB remains unknown, a Robetta-predicted structure is shown in Figure 1A. Sequence comparisons with other homologs and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) measurement of the Fe content suggest that PapB is a SPASM-domain protein and can bind three [4Fe-4S] clusters. The RS cluster activates SAM toward reductive cleavage to form dAdo  (Fig. 1B), which abstracts a H-atom from the C3 of the Asp residue to generate a substrate radical (Fig. 1C). Extended X-ray absorption fine-structure studies have shown one of the two ACs is responsible for binding and activating Cys thiol of the CX3D motif. The formation of the thioether cross-link that oxidizes the C3 of Asp and generates a single electron is followed by disengagement of the sulfur from the cluster. It has been proposed that this electron is stored in AC1. Currently, the role of the third cluster, AC2, is unknown, but it is possible that AC1 and AC2 may collectively be involved in the reactivation of the RS cluster. As with many other rSAM enzymes where a reducing equivalent remains in the active site of the enzyme at the end of the catalytic cycle, it is thought that the electron will return to the RS cluster, thereby reactivating the enzyme for the next round of catalysis. Indeed, in several systems where it has been examined, prereduction of the enzyme is sufficient to permit multiple turnovers to occur without the addition of exogenous reducing equivalents. In general, the reactivation of these prereduced systems is thought to occur by electron transfer back to the RS cluster, although there is no direct evidence for whether the transfer is intra- or intermolecular.

The true biological mechanism behind the two reduction steps necessary for the activation and post-catalysis reactivation of the RS cluster in PapB and other rSAM enzymes are enigmatic. Current hypotheses suggest that the first step may require flavodoxin or flavodoxin-like systems for the reductive activation in vivo. However, the Booker study discussed above suggests that one cannot eliminate the possibility that in vivo reduction may not require a dedicated protein or class of enzymes. The second elusive step is the postcatalysis reactivation in rSAM enzymes that house multiple clusters, where the catalytic cycle returns the reducing equivalent back to the RS cluster to rearm it. Intramolecular electron transfer has often been invoked for this step, however, without evidence.

This study explores the reductive activation of PapB and the fate of the electron that remains in the protein at the end of the catalytic cycle. In contrast to current models, our findings suggest that intermolecular electron transfer is necessary for each cycle of PapB to return the reducing equivalent back to the RS cluster to ready the system for another cycle. The studies described below include variants of PapB where each of the three clusters is deleted to provide evidence that the intermolecular electron transfer requires AC2. Our results support a new paradigm for the cellular activation of rSAM enzymes, as they show no specific activator is necessary. We demonstrate that, under anaerobic conditions, NADPH can reduce flavin mononucleotide (FMN), which in turn activates PapB. As proof of concept for intermolecular electron transfer, we present evidence for the transfer between two completely unrelated rSAM enzymes, one that is prereduced and the other oxidized. Under this scenario, we see reciprocal reductive activation of both systems when assayed in situ. These results suggest that the true biological reduction of rSAM may occur in more ways than considered previously as it does not require a specific biological reducing partner, but instead, it only needs one that can deliver the reducing equivalent in one-electron steps. The implications of these findings will be discussed in the context of a generalized model for the in vivo reductive activation of rSAM enzymes.
Results
Purification of PapB

PapB (~55 kDa) was purified to homogeneity from an overexpressing E. coli strain (Fig. S1) and reconstituted with iron and sulfide as described. Amino acid and ICP-MS analysis of enzyme purified from three separate rounds of expression revealed that the protein contains 13.5 +- 0.3 mol of iron per mol of PapB. Sequence alignments with CteB (PDB:5WGG) and anSME (PDB:4K37) show that PapB conserves the 10 Cys residues that bind RS, AC1, and AC2 in CteB and anSME (Fig. S2). In the Robetta analysis of PapB, these Cys residues are grouped in such manner as to support binding of the RS cluster (red), AC1 (yellow), and AC2 (purple) (Fig. 1). The iron content of reconstituted PapB used in the studies described below is sufficient to support formation of three [4Fe-4S] clusters.
PapB is active in the absence of FPR

Dependence of the activity of PapB on components of the reducing system. PapB is fully active in the buffer solutions that contain FldA, FPR, SAM, and NADPH (see Fig. S3), with quantitative cross-linking of msPapA observed in 15 min. In a charge state of +3, a cross-link corresponds to a shift of -0.6719, which is a Delta2 Da (m/z = 843.4478, M = 2530.3434). A, control reactions with no SAM or (B) NADPH show only trace quantities of cross-linked peptide. C, by contrast, ~40% completion is observed in the absence of FldA. D, nearly quantitative conversion to the cross-linked species is observed in the absence of FPR. The red dotted line signifies the unmodified monoisotopic mass of the msPapA peptide (m/z = 844.1197, M = 2532.3591).

The catalytic activity of PapB was readily assessed by analyzing the msPapA peptide by LC-MS for cross-linking after incubating with PapB, SAM, and either the reducing system of 2 mM NaDT or 25 muM FldA, 2 muM FPR, and 2 mM NADPH. It should be noted that all the assay mixtures also contained 2 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) to minimize the dimerization of the peptide by the formation of disulfides. A representative mass spectrometry (MS) (in positive ion mode) of the peptide in the presence and absence of full assay components is shown in Fig. S3. Figure 2 shows the z = 3 charge state of the msPapA peptide after incubation with PapB for 15 min under various conditions. The thioether modification led to a Delta2 amu in the m/z of the monoisotopic peak. Throughout this study, the extent of cross-linking is determined by comparisons of the intensity of the monoisotopic peak of the cross-linked species to the peak in the envelope that has contributions from the monoisotopic peak of the unmodified peptide (see Fig. S4 for simulated envelopes corresponding to 0%-100% turnover). In the presence of NADPH, FPR, FldA, and SAM, the msPapA substrate is quantitatively converted to the cross-linked species (Fig. S3). When SAM is excluded (Fig. 2A), a small amount of turnover is also observed, likely from the endogenous SAM from the E. coli expression host that copurifies with the protein. Furthermore, when NADPH is removed from the assay reaction (Fig. 2B), a small amount of cross-linked msPapA was observed. We attributed this to the presence of a small amount of prereduced PapB or FldA. Surprisingly, when either FldA (Fig. 2C) or FPR (Fig. 2D) was omitted from the reactions, significant amounts of cross-linked msPapA are observed. In the absence of FldA, ~45% of the starting msPapA is transformed to product in 180 min, whereas in the absence of FPR, 100% conversion is observed.

The turnover observed in the absence of FPR is unexpected. To our knowledge, there is no evidence in the literature that FldA can be reduced by pyridine nucleotides. We posit that the activity results from either a small fraction of the purified FPR (or FldA) existing in the reduced form or their presence allows for the small amount of activity that is observed in the absence of NADPH (Fig. 2B) to become amplified. We cannot exclude the possibility that a small fraction of the PapB is purified in its reduced state and responsible for this background activity. It is also possible the DTT in these assays is reducing FldA or FPR, thereby furnishing a source of reducing equivalents for PapB; however, this reduction is slow and in controls described below not significant in the 3-h timeframe of the experiment. Moreover, such a DTT-dependent reduction does not explain the substantial amount of additional turnover seen when comparing samples lacking NADPH with those that did not contain either FldA or FPR (compare Fig. 2C or Fig. 2, B-D). These latter observations point to a role for NADPH even in the absence of FdA or FPR.
PapB activity with FMN and NADPH

PapB is active in the presence of FMN and NADPH.A, in the absence of PapB, no cross-linking is observed (top row). Full cross-linking of the peptide substrate is seen after 3 h when FMN and NADPH are present (bottom row). B, when NADPH is excluded, PapB still cross-links msPapA, albeit inefficiently. C, by contrast to (A and B) where FMN is present, removing FMN from the assay mixture leads to the formation of <1% cross-linked msPapA. The red dashed lines denote the calculated unmodified monoisotopic mass of msPapA (m/z = 844.1197).

Both FPR and FldA are flavoenzymes. To gain additional insights into the mechanism by which either FldA or FPR can support turnover, activity assays with PapB were carried out in the presence of FMN and NADPH (Fig. 3). Remarkably, in the presence of FMN and excess NADPH, we observe the quantitative conversion of msPapA to the cross-linked product (Fig. 3A). Alternatively, in the absence of NADPH, this activity is minimal, with only ~30% of the substrate being cross-linked even after 180 min of incubation (Fig. 3B). As with the experiments shown in Figure 2, 2 mM DTT is included in these assays; therefore, the residual activity could result from reduction of PapB by DTT-reduced FMN. Interestingly, in the absence of FMN there is no measurable product formed (Fig. 3C), clearly establishing that the flavin cofactor is the likely conduit of electrons from NADPH to PapB. NADPH is an obligatory hydride donor, and therefore, it is not surprising that it is unable to support turnover of PapB in the absence of a one-electron donor.
FMN or FldA can be reduced by NADPH

FldA and FMN are reduced in the presence of NADPH. A solution containing (A) 55 muM FldA or (B) FMN was incubated with 2 mM NADPH and spectra were obtained over a period of 180 min. While the flavin is reduced in both cases, the spectral changes in (A) suggest that FldA is reduced to the semiquinone, likely from equilibration of oxidized and two-electron reduced. FMN is reduced to the hydroquinone form. Each experiment was carried out in triplicate, but (A and B) show a representative example.

The above results implicate NADPH-reduced FldA (or FMN) in the activation of PapB. To assess this, we carried out assays in which 60 muM FldA or FMN was incubated with 2 mM NADPH in 50 mM Pipes NaOH (pH 7.4) containing 300 mM KCl and the UV-visible spectra were monitored over 180 min (Fig. 4). Control experiments in the presence of 2 mM DTT in place of NADPH are shown in Fig. S5. In the presence of NADPH, FldA is reduced to the semiquinone species (Fig. 4A) and FMN to the hydroquinone (Fig. 4B). Within the 180-min timeframe, neither FldA (Fig. S5A) nor FMN (Fig. S5B) is reduced in the presence of 2 mM DTT (Fig. S5). To our knowledge, the ability of NADPH to directly reduce FMN or FldA has not been reported previously and may reflect the strictly anaerobic conditions employed in the assays; these results are highly significant as they allow for a new paradigm for the reductive activation of rSAM enzymes. The fact that PapB activity is observed when either FldA or FMN is present along with NADPH suggests that either the hydroquinone or semiquinone state of FMN can reduce the RS cluster of PapB to initiate catalysis (see Figs. 2 and 3). Our interpretation of the difference in the fate of flavin bound to FldA and free in solution is that, in both cases, the hydroquinone is the initial product, but with FldA, reduced FldA in the hydroquinone state can reduce oxidized FldA generating two equivalents of Fld with bound semiquinone.

In our interpretation of the data presented in Figures 2 and 3, we could not account fully for the PapB activity that is observed when NADPH was removed from assays containing FPR/FldA (Fig. 3B) or FldA (Fig. 2B). Considering that the control experiment shows the inability of 2 mM DTT alone to reduce FMN, even after 3 h (Fig. S5), the observed residual activities can be rationalized only if the oxidized flavin (either in FldA or FMN in solution) is playing a previously undetermined electron transfer role that is stimulatory.
Oxidized FldA and FMN stimulate activity of prereduced PapB

The reaction catalyzed by PapB should be redox neutral. Once the RS cluster is reduced, PapB reductively cleaves SAM to generate dAdo , which in turn initiates the chemistry by H-atom transfer from the substrate. Upon formation of the thioether cross-link, which oxidizes the C3 of Asp, the reducing equivalent is returned to the enzyme, presumably to AC1 based on the previously published selenocysteine (SeCys) peptide substitution that demonstrated direct binding and subsequent disengagement from an AC during selenoether formation. Therefore, one would expect that the enzymatic system would need to be primed once by prereduction and that subsequent turnover cycles would not require additional external reducing equivalents. To assess this, we reduced PapB in the presence of 10 mM NaDT after purification and reconstitution. The excess NaDT was removed by gel filtration, and the protein was concentrated before further chromatography using a high-resolution gel filtration column. A sample of the flow-through from the concentration step was kept as a control for experiments described later. In the experiments described below, a msPapA variant containing Y17W substitution was employed to permit a more accurate quantitation of the peptide stock. Fig. S6 shows the mass spectrum of an assay utilizing the Y17W msPapA after incubation with prereduced PapB. The data show that prereduced PapB is marginally catalytically active, as evidenced by the conversion of ~3% of substrate to the cross-linked product in 2 h. Additionally, there is a time-dependent increase in the cross-linked product over the 18-h incubation (Figs. 5 and S6). The notable observation here is that, while the prereduced protein is catalytically active, the activity is not as robust as when the protein is assayed in the presence of excess reductant. Previously, we reported the estimated turnover number of PapB as 7.4 +- 0.1 s-1 when assayed in the presence of NaDT and 2.6 +- 0.2 s-1 when reduced by FldA/FPR/NADPH, when acting on the Y17W peptide as the substrate. While the activity with the prereduced enzyme is lower, we suspect that the reduction is not quantitative and only a small fraction of the PapB is reduced with NaDT in the prereduction conditions.

Prereduced PapB can cross-link Y17W msPapA and is more efficient in the presence of either oxidized FldA or oxidized FMN. The assays contained 450 muM Y17W msPapA, 1.9 muM prereduced PapB, 2 mM DTT, and 2.4 mM SAM. The assays with electron mediators contained 25 muM of either oxidized FMN (green square) or FldA (red triangle). Each experiment was carried out in triplicate and all replicates are shown. For mass spectra of sample withdrawn at 2, 4, 6, and 18 h, see Fig. S5 for prereduced PapB, Fig. S6 for prereduced PapB + FldA(ox), and Fig. S7 for prereduced PapB + FMN(ox).

In the experiments shown in Figure 3, oxidized flavin (in solution or bound as in FldA/FPR) stimulates the activity of PapB. To determine the source of the stimulation, assays with the prereduced PapB were carried out in the presence of either oxidized FldA or FMN. Remarkably, the reaction rate is twice as fast in the case of FldA and more than 3 times as fast with FMN compared with prereduced PapB alone (see Fig. 5 for percent turnover for each respective scenario, and see Figs. S7 and S8 for MS spectra for each timepoint for the FldA and FMN scenarios, respectively). While the reaction remains slow with the prereduced enzyme, we observed complete conversion of the msPapA to the modified form in 18 h in the presence of either FldA or FMN. This is consistent with observations in Figure 3B, which show that inclusion of FMN alone leads to measurable, albeit slow, activity.

Our working mechanism for the activity of PapB is that the formation of the cross-linked product generates a singly reduced PapB, where the electron presumably resides in AC1. Therefore, to ready the system for a second round of catalysis, the electron must be cycled back to the RS cluster. The mechanism by which this electron is returned to the RS cluster is unknown. It has been proposed that this transfer is intramolecular. The results described above with assays containing FldA and FMN suggested to us that the process may be intermolecular. That is, for the electron to cycle back to the RS cluster, it must first be transferred from the protein to an external recipient.

To obtain evidence that intermolecular electron cycling is possible, at least in principle, prereduced PapB was incubated in the presence of another RS enzyme, 6-carboxy-6-deazaguanine synthase (QueE, Uniprot O31677), which, as purified, is catalytically inactive. QueE is a class 1 rSAM enzyme and catalyzes the conversion of 6-carboxy-5,6,7,8-tetrahydropterin (CPH4) to CDG (see Fig. S9) in the biosynthetic pathway to deazapurine-containing natural products. QueE has been extensively characterized and contains a single 4Fe-4S cluster, which binds and upon reduction to the +1 state activates the SAM for reductive cleavage to form dAdo . The dAdo  initiates the catalytic cycle by H-atom transfer from the substrate. The reaction catalyzed by QueE is catalytic in SAM, as the cofactor is reformed upon formation of CDG. Prereduced PapB was assessed for its ability to activate oxidized as-isolated QueE. To ensure that the prereduced PapB sample did not have any residual reductant, the flow-through of the final concentration step (see above) was added to an assay mixture containing both CPH4 and msPapA substrates, as well as all the other assay components except for a reducing equivalent (Fig. 6, top row). An aliquot of this reaction mixture was analyzed by HPLC interfaced to both an MS and a UV-visible detector. The UV-visible and MS spectra of the species eluting at 7.9 min are consistent with CPH4, and there is no evidence for CDG in either chromatogram. Additionally, msPapA is unmodified, consistent with the modification requiring PapB, which is not present in the assay. Next, as a positive control, an identical reaction was set up containing 2 mM NaDT (Fig. 6, middle row). In this sample, the CPH4 is converted to CDG, as evidenced by the appearance of a new peak at 8.9 min with a UV-visible feature at 300 nm, as well as a species with m/z of ~195.05 in the MS trace (Fig. 6, middle row, blue MS). As in the reaction containing the flow-through, there is no modification to msPapA because no PapB is present (Fig. 6, middle row, green MS). In the identical assay containing PapB (Fig. 6, bottom row), a peak in the HPLC traces consistent with CDG exhibiting a peak at 300 nm in the UV-visible trace and a m/z of 195.05 in the corresponding MS are observed. In contrast to the controls above, in the presence of prereduced PapB, msPapA is modified as well, evidenced by the 2 Da shift in the peptide MS envelope (Fig. 6, bottom row, green MS). Generally, these experiments show in principle PapB can transfer reducing equivalents to an unrelated electron acceptor (QueE), providing the first unambiguous evidence for intermolecular electron transfer between two unrelated rSAM proteins.

Additionally, the intermolecular activation experiment was carried out in reverse direction, where prereduced QueE was mixed with oxidized PapB under the same reaction conditions above. When the concentrations of PapB and QueE were held constant, no cross-linked msPapA was observed after 18 h (Fig. S10A). However, when the ratio of QueE:PapB was 10:1, approximately 50% of the Y17W msPapA was cross-linked after 18 h (Fig. S10B). This differential ability of QueE to pass reducing equivalents to PapB likely reflects the difference in the midpoint potentials of the proteins, which potentially favors localization on QueE. The reciprocal activation of QueE and PapB suggests that these rSAM enzymes are capable of exchanging electrons. Taken together with the activation of PapB with FMN/NADPH, or MiaB with ferredoxin-NADP+ oxidoreductase, it is plausible that, in vivo, redox active enzymes could activate rSAM enzymes. These observations also provide an explanation for the stimulatory effect of oxidized FldA or FMN observed in Figures 2 and 3, as either one can play a role in shuttling the reducing equivalent post catalysis to the RS cluster.
Role of [4Fe-4S] clusters of PapB in intermolecular electron transfer

Based on sequence alignments (Fig. S2), predicted structures (Fig. 1A), and iron content, PapB can house three [4Fe-4S] clusters, any of which may be capable of reducing QueE. We do not know where the electron introduced during the prereduction resides in the protein, and therefore we could not determine which of the three clusters may be involved in the electron transfer to QueE. Therefore, three site-directed variants of PapB were generated: DeltaRS, DeltaAC1, and DeltaAC2. Cys-to-Ala variants were constructed by site-directed mutagenesis, which removed all the putative coordinating Cys residues for each variant. The Cys to Ala mutations are as follows: DeltaRS (C119, C123, and C126); DeltaAC1 (C352, C370, and C421); and DeltaAC2 (C408, C411, C417, and C440). Unlike WT PapB, which is highly stable and is readily obtained in pure form, these variants are substantially less stable (Fig. S11). We encountered significant difficulties while removing the purification tag after TEV cleavage, as the PapB variants became unstable and precipitated during elution from the HisTrap, which was used to separate the TEV-cleaved MBP from PapB. Therefore, the MBP tags were not cleaved in the subsequent studies with the mutants. SDS-PAGE analysis of the variants shows three major species: the higher-molecular-weight band (~100 kDa) corresponds to the full-length MBP-PapB, and the lower-molecular-weight bands suggest significant cleavage of the MBP from PapB yielding the isolated tag alone (~42 kDa) and PapB (~54 kDa). ICP-MS analysis of the samples and comparison with the protein concentration from the Bradford assays indicates that the protein variants contain 2 +- 0.8 equivalents of Fe per mol of polypeptide, which suggests only a partial reconstitution had occurred.

The DeltaRS, DeltaAC1, or DeltaAC2 variants were assessed for catalytic activity. When incubated with SAM under reducing conditions, the DeltaRS variant did not produce any dAdo, whereas both the DeltaAC1 and DeltaAC2 variants did (Fig. S12). Interestingly, while the MS spectra of the msPapA peptide revealed no cross-link with the DeltaRS or DeltaAC1 variants, the AC2 variant produces a small but measurable quantity of cross-linked product. The dAdo formation being reliant on the RS cluster is consistent with all established data with rSAM enzymes. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of an AC2 knockout that still produces the anticipated cross-linked product.

While the AC2 variant appears to be catalytically active, the enzyme only carries out a single turnover. Based on the ratio of modified to unmodified peptide in the MS, the same quantity of cross-linked product was formed in the reactions containing 1:1, 2:1, or 4:1 ratio of msPapA:DeltaAC2 PapB after an 18-h incubation (Fig. S13). In each reaction no more than 10 muM of the msPapA is turned over. Since the concentration of DeltaAC2 PapB was 40 muM in each assay, these data suggest that approximately one-fourth of the protein is fully reconstituted. Furthermore, the observation that the protein produces the same quantity of cross-linked product regardless of concentration of msPapB suggests that the stoichiometry of the reaction is limited by the PapB variant.

In all the cases, a small amount of methylthioadenosine is observed resulting from nonenzymatic hydrolysis of SAM. In the presence of NaDT, CDG is observed, consistent with the ability of NaDT to fully activate QueE. In the presence of prereduced PapB, CDG is formed in all samples. However, the amount of CDG produced is reduced in the DeltaRS and DeltaAC2 samples relative to the DeltaAC1 samples.
